document_title: UPDATE. Bristol Bay's newest salmon counter listens
post_copy:
On the Wood River a person on a tower clicks each passing salmon by hand, and on the Naknek near King Salmon a sonar will listen.

The tower count goes back to 1955. Crews at nine Fish and Game sites click in 10 minute intervals around the clock.

The sonar is new. BBRSDA announced a $188,268 NFWF award on October 29th, National Fisherman reports. It is meant to count returning salmon automatically and feed an online dashboard.

The Wood tower's 2,586,432 sockeye this year sat inside the river's goal.

What the grant funds and where. How the sonar listens across the river and the clicker count it joins. The 2026 run drawn as marks, the three counters side by side and the Wood River tower count against its goal.

If you fish or buy fish on the Naknek, would you trust an in-season machine count before anyone grades it against a tower?

#BristolBay #SockeyeSalmon #FisheriesTech

slides.headline: On the Naknek, the newest salmon counter listens.
A federal grant puts an automated sonar near King Salmon.
slides.body: BBRSDA announced the NFWF award of $188,268 on October 29th, National Fisherman reports. The sonar is meant to count returning salmon automatically and feed an online dashboard. The Naknek is its first site. The grant runs June 1st to May 31st, 2028.

slides.headline: It listens across a wide stretch of the river.
slides.body: "Sonar lets us count fish across a wide stretch of the Naknek," says Lilani Dunn of BBRSDA. SeaSignal Technologies, working with Coastal Measures and BioSonics, was picked to build and run it, per National Fisherman.

slides.headline: From the riverbed to a screen, during the season.
slides.body: Across the bay, most counts are still made by hand.

slides.headline: Since 1955, a person and a hand clicker.
slides.body: Most Bristol Bay escapement counts come from nine Fish and Game tower sites. Crews rotate through shifts around the clock and click each passing salmon in 10 minute intervals.

slides.headline: 45.7 million sockeye came back to Bristol Bay this year. 15.6 million made it upriver to spawn.

slides.kicker: THREE COUNTERS, AS EACH SOURCE DESCRIBES THEM
slides.headline: One fishery, three ways to count.
slides.body: NOAA and NFWF's 2026 slate funded 13 grants, $3.4 million, with $4.2 million matched. As of July, Fish and Game wasn't directly involved in the drone pilot.

slides.headline: Wood River's tower counted 2,586,432 sockeye this year.
slides.body: Fish and Game's goal there is 700,000 to 2,800,000. The Kvichak, Naknek, Alagnak, Egegik and Wood were all inside their goals. The drone pilot is set to be compared against tower counts like this one.

slides.headline: Should the Naknek's machine count go live in season, or be checked against a tower first?

editor_notes_for_email: This edition is an UPDATE of No.2 and No.77 on machine counting in Bristol Bay, now with the Naknek sonar award. The caption is carried byte for byte with no factual flags. The two grant figures, $188,300 on the NFWF 2026 slate for the Wood River drone and AI pilot and $188,268 reported by National Fisherman for the Naknek sonar, are shown side by side on slide 7, each attributed to its own source, and nothing on the caption, slides or sources comment claims they are one award or that the scope changed. Every Naknek sonar detail rests on National Fisherman alone (bbrsda.com/news returned empty), so it is attributed wherever it appears. The ADF&G 2026 figures are preliminary.
